content: To effectively monitor and integrate data on the delivery of community-based health services, it is essential to capture information from mobile or satellite clinics, often operated by peer or outreach workers. These services are particularly critical for high-risk populations who may not otherwise access healthcare facilities. Without incorporating data from these community-based services into routine systems, significant gaps in understanding the coverage and quality of service delivery to these populations will persist. National HIV monitoring and evaluation frameworks should include data from multiple sources, utilized at various management levels. Key data sources include voluntary counseling and testing centers, hospital ART clinics, vital statistics registries, private physicians, and clinics focused on preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission. These sources should be linked with unique identifiers to ensure comprehensive tracking. Core data elements collected in primary tools often serve multiple purposes, such as patient care, program management, and monitoring. Indicators must be regularly reviewed to ensure the data collected is relevant and actionable. For example, monitoring ART program functionality involves tracking key milestones like HIV diagnosis, CD4 testing, ART initiation, viral load suppression, and mortality. The WHO 2020 strategic information guidelines emphasize tracking the HIV service cascade, which visualizes critical outputs and outcomes of the health sector's response to the epidemic. This cascade, anchored by the 95-95-95 targets for 2030, identifies trends, progress, gaps, and bottlenecks in service delivery. Strengthening data analysis at each stage of the cascade, from prevention to viral suppression, is crucial for improving outcomes. Routine monitoring of antiretroviral (ARV) drug toxicity is vital, especially with the transition to dolutegravir (DTG) as the preferred first-line ART. This transition offers opportunities to optimize treatment but also introduces risks of new drug-related toxicities. Monitoring should focus on treatment-limiting toxicities, defined as life-threatening illnesses, hospitalizations, or adverse drug reactions leading to drug discontinuation or substitution. Longitudinal monitoring is recommended to address emerging concerns, such as excessive weight gain associated with DTG use, and to assess metabolic comorbidities, cardiovascular risks, and maternal outcomes. The WHO has developed tools to support countries in implementing active toxicity monitoring and integrating it with pharmacovigilance systems. Data from clinical trials and cohort studies highlight the need for longitudinal monitoring of body weight, metabolic health, and other risk factors among people living with HIV. HIV drug resistance is a growing global concern, particularly with the emergence of resistance to NNRTIs and NRTIs. Resistance compromises ART effectiveness and threatens sustained reductions in HIV-related morbidity and mortality. The 2019 WHO global report documented high levels of pretreatment resistance to efavirenz (EFV) and nevirapine (NVP) in several lowand middle-income countries, exceeding 10% in some regions. Resistance levels were notably higher among women and individuals with prior ARV exposure. The clinical impact of HIV drug resistance is significant, leading to poorer outcomes and necessitating rapid transitions to second-line ART when viral load suppression fails. Resistance to tenofovir and dual resistance to tenofovir and other NRTIs further complicate treatment strategies. While resistance to dolutegravir remains low, efforts to prevent its emergence should be prioritized. WHO recommends that countries develop national action plans to address HIV drug resistance, integrating these plans into broader HIV strategies. Key activities include monitoring quality-of-care indicators, conducting periodic surveys of acquired and pretreatment resistance, and ensuring access to child-friendly, non-NNRTI-based ART formulations. These efforts are critical to maintaining the effectiveness of ART and achieving global HIV targets.
